cf.title: Keep TIDBitmap pagetable memory across bitmap scans

input.subject: Keep TIDBitmap pagetable memory across bitmap scans

verdict_reasoning: The contention is measured and the problem is stated well, but the case for a tidbitmap-only cache is open at level 1b. Message #3 shows that setting both glibc thresholds removes the faults in every tested node and leaves the patch a 5.5% to 11.8% gain (already-exists-1). The author agrees there that a process-wide fix is the better target. All numbers are at 96 clients on one synthetic workload (demand-2).

brief.title: Keep TIDBitmap pagetable memory in a per-backend cache across bitmap scans
brief.problem: Large bitmap heap scans regrow the TIDBitmap simplehash pagetable from 256 slots each query, and glibc trims the freed heap at ExecutorEnd, so the next query page-faults the same memory again (about 730 faults per query). With many concurrent backends, these faults and trims contend on a shared kernel page LRU lock, and the author measured a third of CPU in system time at 96 clients. Planner-based presizing fails when estimates are wrong, as with GIN array containment.
brief.proposed_design: 0002 keeps the pagetable array and sorted page list of up to two large private bitmaps per backend in a "TIDBitmap cache" memory context. A bitmap that reaches 2048 slots takes a free entry and switches to its array, and a reset callback on the bitmap's context returns the entry on error. Total retained memory is capped at work_mem, with no idle release; 0001 adds a test module.
user_visible_surface: New memory context "TIDBitmap cache" visible in pg_backend_memory_contexts.
Per-backend retained memory up to work_mem after a large bitmap scan, until a smaller-work_mem bitmap scan or backend exit.
author_claims: At 96 clients with glibc defaults, TPS rises 34.8% to 64.9% and page faults per query drop to 0.
Under musl, gains are +63.8% (btree) and +88.9% (BitmapAnd); under jemalloc +4.7% to +11.9%.
Contention is on a per-NUMA-node page queue lock, seen on Linux with and without memcg and on FreeBSD.
Setting both glibc M_TRIM_THRESHOLD and M_MMAP_THRESHOLD at backend start removes the faults process-wide; the patch still adds 5.5% to 11.8% on top.
Hash join and sort show the same fault pattern; the patch does not help them.
brief.thread_state: David Geier agrees memory should be kept but objects to doing it in tidbitmap.c, citing memory use with many connections and other doubling allocations. Greg agreed a process-wide allocator fix is the better target; whether this patch should proceed is open, and the last message is truncated.
unclear: The patch text is not readable, so the actual code changes cannot be checked.
The author does not say whether he will continue this patch or switch to a mallopt or allocator-level patch.
The reproducer scripts are not posted.
No numbers are given for a work_mem far above the default with many backends.
The truncated last message's conclusion on sbrk trimming within one statement is not visible.

prior_attempts.title: Add GUC to tune glibc's malloc behaviour
prior_attempts.quote: I think your approach is fundamentally overfitting our code to a specific malloc implementation, in a way that's not tunable by mere mortals. It just seems like a dead end to me.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane objected that such a GUC means nothing on non-glibc platforms, and he suggested documenting the glibc environment variables instead. Andres Freund held that the patch overfits Postgres to one malloc implementation in a way users cannot tune. He argued that Postgres should control allocation itself in aset.c and the other memory contexts, because the cost comes from page faults and zeroing new pages. The CF manager returned the entry because no update addressed these objections.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 tuned glibc through mallopt with a GUC. This patch keeps memory inside tidbitmap.c and works on any libc, but message #3 suggests a backend-start mallopt fix that is close to P1.

objections.title: Most of the gain is available today through glibc malloc environment variables
objections.failure_scenario: An operator on glibc sets MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_ and MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_ in the postmaster environment and gets 4,040 TPS with no faults. tidbitmap.c then carries a permanent per-backend cache that adds about 6% on top of that. Hash join and sort also stop faulting under the same setting, and the patch does nothing for them.
objections.argument: Message #3 shows that setting both glibc thresholds removes the faults in every tested node, and that the patch adds only 5.5% to 11.8% on top. glibc reads these thresholds from environment variables, so no code change is needed, and [P1] records the suggestion to document those variables instead of tuning them in core. The author's strongest answer is musl, which has no such knobs (+63.8%). That is a real gap, but it is narrower than the headline numbers suggest.
objections.author_must_show: With both glibc thresholds set, or under jemalloc, which workloads still gain enough to justify a permanent cache in tidbitmap.c, and how many deployments use musl?

precedents.title: Add GUC to tune glibc's malloc behaviour

critic.reasoning: Message #3 shows both glibc thresholds give 4,040 TPS with no faults, and the author calls the remaining gain a much smaller argument. The objection already allows for musl, where no such setting exists.

objections.title: Demand shown only by one synthetic high-concurrency benchmark
objections.failure_scenario: The cache is committed for a 96-client, single-socket, all-cached pgbench case. Most installations run far fewer concurrent large bitmap scans and see little change. They still carry the retained memory and the extra code path.
objections.argument: The only evidence in messages #1 and #3 is the author's benchmark: 16M rows, about 17k pages per bitmap, 96 clients. The material has no field reports, no -general or -bugs threads, and no numbers at low or moderate concurrency. David Geier's earlier presizing measurement in message #1 comes from the same development work, so it does not show user demand.
objections.author_must_show: What gain does the patch give at 4, 16 and 32 clients, and is there any production report of this kernel lock contention from bitmap scans?

critic.reasoning: The measurements are careful and cover two kernels and several allocators, but all are at 96 clients on one synthetic workload. The thread has no numbers at lower concurrency and no field report.

other_surviving.title: Retained memory changes what work_mem means for idle backends
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A pooled session runs `set work_mem = '1GB'` for a report that uses a large bitmap scan, then resets it. The backend keeps up to 1 GiB until it runs another bitmap scan with a smaller work_mem or exits, and later clients on that backend may never run one. The operator finds the RSS growth only when the host swaps or the OOM killer acts.
other_surviving.argument: Today work_mem limits memory per operation while that operation runs, and users size it on that basis. Message #1 makes it also the cap on memory a backend keeps after the query, with no idle release, and only a later bitmap scan or backend exit gives it back. Message #3 answers the many-connections concern from message #2 only for the default 4 MB. Message #1 itself names a fixed cap below work_mem as the alternative.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How much memory does a backend keep after a session that raised work_mem and then reset it, and why is a work_mem cap better than a small fixed cap?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 confirms the cap is work_mem with no idle release, and only a later bitmap scan with smaller work_mem frees entries. Message #3 answers the concern from message #2 only for the 4 MB default.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Per-module cache for a process-wide allocator problem
other_surviving.failure_scenario: After 0002, hash join and sort still fault about 1,000 times per query under glibc defaults. The next author fixes one of them with a second private cache in nodeHash.c, then a third in tuplesort.c. Each cache has its own cap, threshold and reset callback, and none can see the others' retained memory.
other_surviving.argument: Message #3 shows the same fault pattern in hash join and sort and states that "a process-wide fix is the better target". Message #2 asks for one fix for all doubling allocations. In [P1], the reason recorded was that Postgres should control allocation itself in the memory-context layer. With a process-wide fix in place the patch adds 5.5% to 11.8%, and message #3 calls that "a much smaller argument".
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why should tidbitmap.c keep its own cache rather than having retention done once in the memory-context or allocator layer for all doubling users?

precedents.title: Add GUC to tune glibc's malloc behaviour

critic.reasoning: Message #3 agrees a process-wide fix is the better target and shows hash join and sort are not helped. Fixable, because the author can still argue from the 5.5% to 11.8% rehash gain and the musl numbers.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Design constants tied to glibc defaults and current simplehash
other_surviving.failure_scenario: The radix-tree work replaces the TIDBitmap pagetable, or glibc or simplehash changes its growth behaviour. The 2048-slot threshold and two-entry count stop matching any real boundary. Nothing fails loudly, and the benefit disappears or turns into dead retained memory.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 picks 2048 slots to stay under glibc's 128 kB mmap threshold and to come before simplehash's insert-time grow. It picks two entries to cover BitmapAnd. Message #1 also says the TIDBitmap pagetable is under active redesign in the radix tree thread. A committer would likely ask whether this cache outlives that work.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does this cache relate to the radix tree replacement of the pagetable, and what would detect it when its constants no longer match allocator or simplehash behaviour?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 ties the 2048-slot threshold to the 128 kB mmap threshold and to simplehash's insert-time grow. It defers the relation to the radix tree work to a later follow-up, so the thread has no answer yet.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Per-module cache where a general allocation fix is the stated target
refuted.failure_scenario: After this lands, hash join and sort still fault about 1,000 times per query under glibc defaults. The next author copies the tidbitmap.c pattern into nodeHash.c and tuplesort.c, each keeping up to work_mem per backend with no idle release. A site with many connections then finds retained memory several times larger than expected, spread over separate caches with separate rules.
refuted.argument: The earlier mallopt GUC [P1] was returned partly because, per its thread summary, the fix belonged in Postgres's own memory contexts as a whole, not in one corner. Message #2 makes the same point here, and in message #3 the author agrees a process-wide fix is the better target. Once that fix exists, this patch adds only 5.5% to 11.8%. So the case for a tidbitmap-only cache depends on whether a general fix is expected soon.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should a tidbitmap-only cache go in first, rather than a memory-context-level retention that also covers hash join and sort?

precedents.title: Add GUC to tune glibc's malloc behaviour

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which makes the same point about a tidbitmap-only cache with more direct quotes from messages #2 and #3.

refuted.title: Retained memory scales with work_mem and never decays
refuted.failure_scenario: A site runs 1,000 pooled connections with work_mem = '256MB'. Each backend runs one large bitmap scan, then goes idle. Resident memory grows by up to about 250 GiB and stays there until the backends exit, and the operator finds out when the OOM killer acts.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states there is no idle release and the cap is work_mem. Message #3 answers David's concern from message #2 only for the default 4 MB (800 MB for 200 backends). work_mem is often raised far above the default, and nothing in the thread measures that case. Message #1 mentions a fixed cap below work_mem but does not adopt it.
refuted.author_must_show: What does a backend retain with work_mem in the hundreds of MB, and why is work_mem the right cap rather than a small fixed one?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. Both rest on the work_mem cap with no idle release and on message #3 covering only the default.

refuted.title: A memory cache local to tidbitmap.c duplicates allocator-level retention
refuted.failure_scenario: Later patches fix hash join and sort with their own retained arrays, each capped at work_mem. A backend could then keep several work_mem-sized caches that no allocator can return. Each cache would also need its own reset-callback cleanup.
refuted.argument: Message #2 proposes fixing all doubling allocations in one place, and message #3 agrees that a process-wide fix is the better target. Message #3 also agrees that decay is better done by an allocator. Postgres already decides where to keep memory in its memory-context layer (aset.c and related code), and [P1] records the view that retention belongs there. A second mechanism in one executor node goes against that view, and the proposal justifies it only by the rehash cost.
refuted.author_must_show: Why can the remaining rehash-and-copy gain not come from presizing or from a general memory-context retention policy shared with hash join and sort?

precedents.title: Add GUC to tune glibc's malloc behaviour

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1. The argument about a second retention mechanism outside the memory-context layer is the same point.

refuted.title: Narrow gain once a process-wide allocator fix exists
refuted.failure_scenario: A process-wide fix lands, for example both glibc thresholds set at backend start. tidbitmap.c then still carries its own cache for a 5.5% to 11.8% gain. Hash join and sort authors add their own per-module caches on the same argument, and each one keeps its own memory with its own cap.
refuted.argument: Message #3 shows that setting M_TRIM and M_MMAP_THRESHOLD removes all faults, with stock TPS going from 2,758 to 4,040, against 4,278 patched. The author agrees in message #3 that a process-wide fix is the better target. David Geier in message #2 says other doubling allocations share the mechanism, and message #3 confirms it for hash join and sort. [P1] is an AI summary, but it points the same way: control allocation in the memory-context layer, not in single modules.
refuted.author_must_show: With a process-wide fix in place, which workloads still need the residual rehash-and-copy gain enough to justify a tidbitmap-only cache?

precedents.title: Add GUC to tune glibc's malloc behaviour

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1 and already-exists-1, which between them cover the small remaining gain and the per-module cache concern.

refuted.title: Retained memory falls on all bitmap-scan backends, gain only under contention
refuted.failure_scenario: A site runs 500 connections with work_mem = '64MB' and an occasional large bitmap scan in each backend. Each backend then keeps up to 64 MiB idle until exit, so RSS can grow by about 32 GiB. The operator finds out from OOM kills or swapping, with no setting to turn the cache off.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says the patch has no idle release and caps the cache at work_mem, and offers a fixed cap only as a fallback. David Geier raised the many-connections cost in message #2. The answer in message #3 covers only the 4 MB default, and the brief notes there are no numbers for large work_mem. The cost applies to every backend that ran a large bitmap scan, but the measured gain needs many concurrent ones.
refuted.author_must_show: What is the retained memory and the TPS effect with many backends at a work_mem well above the default, and why is work_mem the right cap?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The retained-memory cost with a large work_mem and many backends is the same concern.

touch_points.reason: 0002 adds a per-backend cache in tidbitmap.c with constants tied to glibc's 128 kB mmap threshold and simplehash growth.

questions: With both glibc thresholds set, or under jemalloc, which workloads still gain enough from the 5.5% to 11.8% rehash saving to justify a cache in tidbitmap.c?
Will you continue this patch, or switch to a process-wide fix that also covers hash join and sort, and how would that fix differ from P1?
What gain does the patch give at 4, 16 and 32 clients, and is there a production report of this lock contention from bitmap scans?
How much memory do many backends keep after a session raised work_mem far above the default, and why is work_mem a better cap than a small fixed one?
How does the cache relate to the radix tree replacement of the pagetable, and do the 2048-slot threshold and two entries still apply after it?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the memory-context layer and tidbitmap.c. No committer has posted in the visible thread; the only reviewer so far objects to the placement.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a per-backend cache with no idle release, capped at work_mem, and for constants that depend on glibc and simplehash behaviour. The cache would also need rework if the radix tree work replaces the pagetable.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered review within a day with new measurements on two kernels and offered the reproducer. He has not said whether he will continue this patch or switch to an allocator-level one.

priority.reason: The goal is valid and well measured, but the thread agrees that a process-wide fix is the better target, and the numbers cover only 96 clients. Review cost is a guess because the patch was not readable; the change is confined to tidbitmap.c and a test module.

provisional_note: The patch text was not readable, so the reset callback, the handling of reused arrays and any change to tidbitmap.h could not be checked. Three level 2 objections on the work_mem cap, the per-module placement and the design constants survived but were not evaluated.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add GUC to tune glibc's malloc behaviour
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a GUC, glibc_malloc_max_trim_threshold, that sets glibc's malloc trim and mmap thresholds through mallopt for each backend. The goal is to stop glibc from returning freed memory to the kernel and taking it back again between queries, which roughly doubled tps in a sort benchmark.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that such a GUC means nothing on non-glibc platforms, and he suggested documenting the glibc environment variables instead. Andres Freund held that the patch overfits Postgres to one malloc implementation in a way users cannot tune. He argued that Postgres should control allocation itself in aset.c and the other memory contexts, because the cost comes from page faults and zeroing new pages. The CF manager returned the entry because no update addressed these objections.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think your approach is fundamentally overfitting our code to a specific malloc implementation, in a way that's not tunable by mere mortals. It just seems like a dead end to me.

precedents_retrieved.title: Adding TRIM_SPACE option to COPY
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a boolean TRIM_SPACE option to COPY FROM, for FORMAT text and csv, that strips leading and trailing spaces from each column value before NULL processing and type conversion. The option is modeled on a similar Snowflake feature and on existing COPY options such as FORCE_NULL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the option adds processing cost to every COPY, used or not, and that COPY should not become a general-purpose filter or ETL tool. Fujii Masao then suggested that only features hard to build outside core belong in COPY, and noted that trimming can be done with COPY PROGRAM. The author offered to withdraw if the general view was that the feature should stay external, and the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
COPY is not a general-purpose filter or ETL tool, and we try
to make it one at our peril.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rename trim_array() for consistency with the rest of array_* functions
precedents_retrieved.summary: Rename trim_array() to array_trim() so it matches the array_* naming of other array functions and shows up in \df array_*. The old name would stay as an undocumented, deprecated alias, to be removed in about 10 years.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Vik Fearing pointed out that the SQL standard mandates TRIM_ARRAY(), so it cannot be deprecated. Michael Paquier suggested leaving things as they are on HEAD, since other functions are likely in the same position, and the author withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
While unfortunately named, we cannot deprecate TRIM_ARRAY() because it
is mandated by the standard.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add numeric_trim(numeric)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Dean Rasheed, Alvaro Herrera, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a function numeric_trim(numeric) that removes trailing zeros after the decimal point by lowering the value's display scale. Reviewers also discussed a minscale() function that returns the smallest scale needed, to be used with round().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed found a bug: numeric_trim(1e100) fails with "value overflows numeric format" because the computed dscale goes negative. He also asked for a simpler implementation based on strip_var(), and the thread moved toward a minscale() design. The author did not post a new version, so Alvaro Herrera and later Robert Haas closed the entry as returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think this patch got useful feedback but we never saw a followup
version posted.  I closed it as returned-with-feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix and improve allocation formulas
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Andres Freund, Michael Paquier
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set fixes two allocation size formulas found with a coccinelle script, in btree_gist and pg_verifybackup. A second, 277kB generated patch rewrites palloc(sizeof(T) * count) calls across the tree as palloc(sizeof(*var) * count), so the size follows the variable's type.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane and Michael Paquier opposed sizeof(*var) as the preferred style, because it hides what is being allocated and a typo like sizeof(*bar) goes undetected, while palloc_object()/palloc_array() let the compiler catch type mismatches. Andres Freund objected to a mass change for its backpatch hazard and review cost, and said the style should be agreed and documented first. Of the two formula fixes, Michael Paquier committed the btree_gist one as 5cf03552fbb4, merged with a fix from another thread, and left the pg_verifybackup uint8-vs-char change for others to comment on.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: IMO what it mostly accomplishes is to remove a cue as to what we are allocating.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use simplehash.h instead of dynahash in SMgr
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the dynahash table that smgr.c uses to look up SMgrRelation entries with a simplehash table, using a small entry that points to the SMgrRelationData, plus a custom hash function; it made recovery about 10% faster in the author's benchmark. Because simplehash does not keep pointers to entries stable, the author later replaced this with a new hash table implementation (generichash) that uses segments and bitmaps.
precedents_retrieved.objection: After the change to a new hash table implementation, Thomas Munro questioned adding another hash table and making the hash table provide fast iteration over its items. The author reports that Andres Freund also opposed the design, saying bitmaps are slow, but those messages are off-list and not shown. With no consensus and no update for two months, the patch no longer applied, and Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Thomas made it quite clear it's not for the patch, and on discussing the patch with Andres, it turned out he does not like the idea either.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add the ability to limit the amount of memory that can be allocated to backends.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch tracks the memory each backend allocates and shows it in pg_stat_activity, and a second patch adds max_total_backend_memory to cap total backend allocations across the cluster. A later version by John Morris keeps local counters in each process and adds them to shared counters from time to time, with error of up to 1 MB per process.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last message shown is a code review from September 2023, and no message covers the 2024 decision. Earlier messages object to widening pg_stat_activity and note that the counts miss OS memory and direct malloc() calls, but nothing shown ties these points to the outcome.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reducing memory usage of creating foreign key between partitioned tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes RelationBuildPartitionDesc build a partitioned table's partition descriptor in a temporary memory context and delete that context afterwards, so the temporary memory is freed instead of being leaked. The aim was to stop the out-of-memory failures seen when adding a foreign key between two partitioned tables that each have thousands of partitions; later revisions were discussed for back-patching to v12.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected early that leak management belongs at the caller level, not inside RelationBuildPartitionDesc. Amit Langote then noted that commit 5b9312378 had already removed the repeated rebuild that caused the leak in v13, so the remaining question was back-patching. Tom Lane found no visible leak in HEAD and saw that the test case was still impractical because of planner cost in RI_Initial_Check, so he saw no reason to back-patch a leak fix. He recommended rejecting the patch and suggested back-porting 5b9312378 instead if a back-branch fix were wanted.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
In short, I don't see a reason why we need this patch in any branch,
so I recommend rejecting it.

roaster_notes.note: The P1 reason does not apply to the patch as posted. It would apply if the thread switches to setting glibc thresholds at backend start.
From the standards angle, the patch adds no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object or pg_dump state. The only user-visible change is the new memory context and the memory it keeps.

The proposal has no persistent or cross-node state: no WAL, on-disk, catalog or wire protocol change, and shared bitmaps for parallel scans are left as before. Without the code it is not possible to check whether exported tidbitmap.h structs or function signatures change for extensions.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect worth objecting to. The cache is private to one backend, so reused arrays never cross a process boundary, and reusing freed memory inside a backend is what aset.c already does. A user can already set work_mem and use that memory during a query, so keeping up to work_mem after the scan gives no new denial-of-service path. The memory cost across many connections belongs to the resource and design angles. Not checked, because the code is not readable: whether a reused array is cleared before it is handed to a new bitmap.
Objections were found; code-level questions such as the reset callback's correctness cannot be checked without readable patches.
Two objections raised; the musl case is a real gap that existing glibc settings cannot cover.
The kernel contention is real and measured. The open question is demand for a tidbitmap-specific fix rather than a general one.
